mcqs.question: What's the key difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore used for mutual exclusion?
options: A mutex can only be used once, while a semaphore can be reused indefinitely
A mutex has ownership — only the locking thread can unlock it — while any thread can signal a semaphore
A binary semaphore is always faster than a mutex
A mutex can protect multiple resources, but a semaphore can only protect one
mcqs.explanation: The defining difference is ownership: a mutex enforces that only the thread that locked it can unlock it, while a semaphore is just a counter that any thread can increment regardless of who decremented it. Neither is inherently faster, both are reusable, and both can be used in whatever scope the programmer designs.

mcqs.question: In the bounded-buffer producer-consumer solution using two semaphores plus a mutex, what is the mutex actually protecting?
options: The count of how many items are in the buffer
The producer thread from running at the same time as the consumer thread under any circumstance
The buffer's internal pointers/indices during the actual read or write of an item
Nothing — it's only there so the code compiles
mcqs.explanation: The mutex guards the brief moment of actually manipulating the buffer's internal state (head/tail pointers, the slot being written or read) so that two threads never corrupt it with a torn read/write. The semaphores, not the mutex, handle the slot-availability counting. Producers and consumers are allowed to run concurrently — that's the whole point of the buffer — just not touch buffer internals at the same instant.

mcqs.question: A semaphore is initialized to 0. Thread A calls wait() and thread B calls signal() once some setup finishes. What is this pattern primarily used for?
options: Protecting a critical section from concurrent access
Enforcing an ordering — making thread A wait until an event in thread B has happened
Implementing a reentrant lock
Limiting the number of concurrent threads to zero
mcqs.explanation: A semaphore starting at 0 with one wait() and one signal() is the classic signaling pattern: it establishes an ordering constraint (B's event happens before A proceeds) with no shared data being protected. It isn't mutual exclusion, has nothing to do with reentrant locking, and doesn't limit concurrency to zero threads — it's a one-shot gate.

mcqs.question: A team uses a semaphore initialized to 1 as a makeshift mutex. Due to a bug, one code path calls signal() twice for a single wait(). What happens?
options: The runtime throws an error immediately, since semaphores enforce one signal per wait
Nothing changes — semaphores are immune to this kind of bug
The semaphore's count silently goes above 1, letting an extra thread into the section meant to be exclusive
The program deadlocks immediately
mcqs.explanation: Semaphores have no ownership tracking, so a duplicate or mismatched signal() just quietly changes the count — there's no built-in check to catch it. The result here is the count drifting above 1, letting more threads through than the mutual-exclusion property intended. This is exactly why a real mutex, which does check ownership, is the safer tool for this job.

mcqs.question: 500 application instances each run a connection pool semaphore initialized to 20, against a database configured for a maximum of 100 total connections. What is the likely outcome under load?
options: No issue — semaphores automatically coordinate across separate processes
Only the semaphore's own process is affected, not the database
The application instances will automatically shrink their pool size to fit
The database can be overwhelmed or refuse connections, since the combined pool capacity (10,000) vastly exceeds its configured maximum
mcqs.explanation: A semaphore only limits concurrency within its own process — it has no visibility into other instances or the backend's actual capacity. With 500 instances × 20 each, up to 10,000 connections could be attempted against a database capped at 100, which will overwhelm or reject connections. There's no automatic cross-process coordination or self-shrinking behavior.
